blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Wave:

A wave is a disturbance which transports energy and momentum both from one point to another without the transport of matter.

Wave Classification:

Some important terms connected with wave motion

(1) Wave length ($\lambda$): It is the distance between two successive crest or two successive troughs.

(2) Frequency($f/n)$: Number of cycle (number of complete wavelengths travelled through a point) completed by a particle in unit time.

(3) Time Period (T) : Time taken by wave to travel a distance equal to the wavelength

(4) Amplitude (A) : Maximum displacement of vibrating particle from its equilibrium position.

(5)Angular frequency (ω) : It is defined as,.$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi n$

(6) Phase: Phase is a quantity which contains all information related to any vibrating particle in a wave.

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx)$

$\text{Phase} \Rightarrow (\omega t - kx)$

(7) Angular wave number (k) : Angular wave number or propagation constant is denoted by$k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$. The S.I. unit of ‘k’ is radian/meter.

(8) Wave number($\bar{v}$): It is defined as number of waves in unit length of the wave pattern.

$\bar{v} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{k}{2\pi}$

(9) Wave velocity ($v$):The velocity with which the disturbance travel through the medium is called wave velocity.

$v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ or $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} \Rightarrow V=n \lambda$

blocks.title: Example -1
blocks.question: A transverse wave is described by the equation $y(x, t) = 0.1 \sin(4\pi x - 200\pi t)$.Determine its wavelength and frequency.
blocks.answer:
Solution :

  • By comparing with equation of wave  $y(x, t)=a \sin (k x-\omega t)$
  • Identify the wave number 4o $k = 4\pi$.
  • Angular frequency $\omega = 200\pi$
  • Calculate the wavelength:
$\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = \dfrac{2\pi}{4\pi} = 0.5 \, \text{m}$
  • Identify the angular frequency $\omega = 200\pi$.
  • Calculate the frequency:
$f = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{200\pi}{2\pi} = 100 \, \text{Hz}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Wave Equation and Characteristics of Waves

Equation of Plane Progressive Wave:

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx + \phi)$

If $\phi=0$

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx )$

Note:  If the wave is along –x direction, then there will be plus sign instead of minus sign inside the brackets in the above equation

$y = A \sin(\omega t + kx )$

Particle Velocity ($v_p$) in Plane Progressive Wave

$v_p = A \omega \cos(\omega t - kx)$

Slope of S.H.W. (Simple Harmonic Wave)

$v_p = -v \left( \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)$

$\left|v_p\right|_{\max }=A \omega$

$v_p=$ particle velocity

$v =$ wave velocity

Particle velocity = - (Wave velocity) × (Slope of the tangent at that point on the wave at that instant)

Relation between phase difference, path difference & Time difference

$\dfrac{\Delta \phi}{2\pi} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\lambda} = \dfrac{\Delta t}{T}$

Acceleration of particle in plane progressive wave

$a_p = -A \omega^2 \sin(\omega t - kx)$

$a_p = -\omega^2 y$

modules.name: Energy Power And Intensity of Wave

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Energy Power and Intensity of Waves:

(1)Wave transport energy when they propagate through a medium. The total kinetic energy K associated with moving particles in one wavelength is

$K = \dfrac{1}{4} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2 \quad \mu \rightarrow \text { mass peronit length }$

(2) Each element of the string has potential energy associated with it due to its displacement from the equilibrium position and the restoring forces from neighbouring elements

$U= \dfrac{1}{4} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2$

$E = U + K = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2$

Intensity: It is defined to be the power per unit area carried by a wave. Power is the rate at which energy is transferred by the wave.

$I = \dfrac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area}} \quad \text { Power }=\frac{\text { Energy }}{\text { time }}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu v A^2 \omega^2 / \text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v A^2 \omega^2$

Speed of Mechanical Wave on String

Velocity of Transverse Mechanical Waves: Velocity of a transverse wave propagating along a string having tension T and mass per unit length µ, is given by

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\pi r^2 \rho}}$

Velocity of Transverse Mechanical Waves: Velocity of a transverse wave propagating along a string having tension T and mass per unit length μ,

$v=\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\pi r^2 \rho}}$

Key Points

  • If medium remains same then  $\rho$ and  v is constant .
$ I \propto A^2 \omega^2 \Rightarrow I \propto A^2 n^2 \quad(\omega=2 \pi n)$

  • If medium and frequency both are constant then $ \mathrm{I} \propto \mathrm{~A}^2$
  • If medium is same and  v  is constant then, intensity (I) $\propto \omega^2 A^2 $
  • $\text { Power }=\dfrac{\text { Enegy }}{\text { Time }}$$$
  • Intensity due to point source $ I=\dfrac{P}{4 \pi \mathrm{r}^2}$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Sound Wave:

  • Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves.
  • They propagate through a medium by compressions and rarefactions.
  • Speed of sound depends on the medium's properties such as density and elasticity.
Sound waves can be classified in three groups according to their range of frequencies.

(1) Infrasonic Waves: Longitudinal wave having frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasonic waves.

(2) Sonic Waves/Audible Waves: Longitudinal waves having frequencies lying between 20 Hz-20000 Hz are called audible waves.

(3) Ultrasonic Waves: Longitudinal waves having frequencies above 20000 Hz are called ultrasonic waves.

Equations of sound wave:

(A) Displacement wave form: $\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{s}_{\max } \cos (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t})$

(B) Pressure wave form: $\Delta \mathrm{p}=\Delta \mathrm{p}_{\max } \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{p}_{\max }=\mathrm{Bks}_{\max }$

Speed of Sound Wave:

$\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\text { Elastic property }}{\text { inertial property }}} \quad \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{\rho}}$

(a) In Solids: $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{Y}}{\rho}}$

(b) In Liquids: $\mathrm{v}_{\ell}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{\rho}}}$

Velocity of sound wave in air according to Newton

In isothermal process B (Bulk modulus) = P (Atmospheric pressure)

$\mathrm{v_g}=\sqrt{\dfrac{P}{\rho}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1.01 \times 10^5}{1.3}}=279 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$

However, the experimental value of sound in air is 332 m/s which is much higher than that given by Newton’s formula.

Laplace’s Correction:

In order to remove the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental values of velocity of sound, Laplace modified Newton’s formula assuming that propagation of sound in air is adiabatic process, i.e. $\mathrm{B}=\gamma \mathrm{P}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{7 \times 1.01 \times 10^5}{5 \times 1.3}}=332 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$

Which is in good agreement with the experimental value (332 m/s). This establishes that sound propagates adiabatically through gases.

modules.name: Effect on Speed of Sound Wave ,loudness, Pitch ,Quality

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Effect of various quantities on speed of sound wave:

1. Effect of temperature:

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}} $

$\quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{~T}} $  (Temperature(T) is in Kelvin)

2.Effect of Relative Humidity: With increase in humidity, density of air decreases

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}$

3.Effect of Pressure: $v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M_W}}$

So, pressure has no effect on velocity of sound in a gas as long as temperature remain constant.

4.Effect of Wind: - If air is blowing then the speed of sound changes. If the actual speed of sound is v and the speed of air is w, then the speed of sound in the direction in which air is blowing will be (v + w), and in the opposite direction it will be (v – w).

5.Effect of Frequency: The speed of sound is not affected by frequency. Sound waves of different frequencies travel at the same speed in air, though their wavelengths vary. If the speed depended on frequency, we wouldn’t be able to enjoy orchestras.

Sound is characterised by the following three parameters:

• Loudness • Pitch • Quality/Timbre

• Loudness: The quality of sound on the basis of which, sound is said to be high or low.

It depends on, (a) Shape and size of the source (b) Intensity of sound

According to Weber - Fechner the loudness of a sound of intensity I is given by:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{L} \propto \log _{10} \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~L}_2-\mathrm{L}_1=\Delta \mathrm{L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1} \end{aligned}$

Unit of loudness - decibel (dB)

For zero decibel (0 dB) Loudness, Intensity is called threshold of hearing$(\mathrm{I_0})$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{L}_2-\mathrm{L}_1=\Delta \mathrm{L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1} \\ & \mathrm{~L}-0=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}_0} \\ & \mathrm{~L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}_0}\left(\text { Where } \mathrm{I}_0=10^{-12} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^2\right) \end{aligned}$

Pitch: It is the sensation received by the ear due to frequency and is the characteristic which distinguishes a shrill (or sharp) sound from a grave (or flat) sound.

Quality (or timbre): - It is the sensation received by the ear due to 'waveform’. Two sounds of same intensity and frequency as shown in figure will produce different sensation on the ear if their waveforms are different.

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Principle of Superposition:

$\vec{y}_{\text{net}} = \vec{y}_1 + \vec{y}_2 + \vec{y}_3$

$y_1 = A_1 \sin(\omega t - k x_1)$,$y_2 = A_2 \sin(\omega t - k x_2)$

Resultant Amplitude

$A_{\text{resultant}}=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$

Resultant Intensity

$I \propto A^2$

$I = I_1 + I_2 + 2 \sqrt{I_1} \sqrt{I_2} \cos \Delta \phi$

Interference for Sound Waves :

When the waves emitting from the coherent sources propagating in same direction are superposed over one another, then redistribution of energy takes place in the space and this phenomenon is called as interference.

  • CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE
  • Phase difference $\Delta \phi
=2n\pi$, where n= 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,.....
  • Path difference $\Delta x=
 0, \, \lambda, \, 2\lambda, \, 3\lambda, \ldots, \, n\lambda$
$A_{\text{max}} = A_1 + A_2$

$I_{\text{max}} = \left( \sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2} \right)^2$

  • DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE
  • Phase difference $\Delta \phi
=(2n+1)\pi$, where n= 0,1,2,3,4,5,....
  • Path difference  $\Delta x
 = \frac{\lambda}{2}, \frac{3\lambda}{2}, \frac{5\lambda}{2}, \ldots, \frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{2}$
$A_{\text{min}} = A_1 - A_2$

$I_{\text{min}} = \left( \sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2} \right)^2$

$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\dfrac{A_{\max }}{A_{\min }}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2$

$\text { Average intensity of interference pattern }=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{2}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2$

Degree of interference pattern (f) = f represents contrast effect (clarity of interference pattern)

$\mathrm{f}=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }-\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }} \times 100 \%$

blocks.answer:
$A_{\text{resultant}}=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$

For constructive interference:

ϕ=0, 2π, 4π, 6π,…, 2nπ
$A_{\text{resultant}}=3+4=7$

For destructive interference:

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Beats :When two sound waves of nearly equal (but not exactly equal) frequencies travel in same direction, at a given point due to their superposition, intensity alternatively increases and decreases periodically. This periodic waxing and waning of sound at a given position is called beats.

$\text { Beat frequency } \Delta f=\left|f_2-f_1\right|$

$\text { Beat Time period } T_{\text {beat }}=\dfrac{1}{\left|f_2-f_1\right|}$

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{res}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}_1+\mathrm{f}_2}{2}$

$\text { Time for } I_{\max } \text { to } I_{\min }, t=\dfrac{T_{\text {beat }}}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2\left|f_2-f_1\right|}$

blocks.text:

  • Using incorrect tension or length values without proper calibration.
  • Assuming sound always travels the same path length in both tubes.

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Stationary Waves: When two identical waves (transverse or longitudinal) propagating in opposite direction superimpose in bounded medium then the resultant wave is called stationary wave or standing wave.

It is of two types

(1) Transverse stationary waves

(2) Longitudinal stationary waves

According to the nature of Reflected surface, Reflection are of two types,

(1) Reflection from rigid end

$y_i = a \sin(\omega t - k x)$

$y_r =- a \sin(\omega t + k x)$

The stationary wave formed due to the superposition of the incident and reflected waves is:

$y=y_i+y_r=a \sin (\omega t-k x)-a \sin (\omega t+k x)$

Note: In such type of reflection incident and reflected waves have phase difference of $\pi$ and direction of propagation are opposite

(2) Reflection from free end

$y_i = a \sin(\omega t - k x)$

$y_r = a \sin(\omega t + k x)$

Rigid End Reflection:

$y=2 a \cos (\omega t) \sin (k x)$

Free End Reflection:

$y=2 a \sin (\omega t) \cos (k x)$

Note: In such type of reflection incident and reflected waves are in phase and direction of propagation are opposite.

Important Points:

Nodes are points of zero displacement, and antinodes are points of maximum displacement in a standing wave.

Distance between two successive nodes or successive antinodes is λ/2.

Distance between successive node to antinode or antinode to node is λ/4.

modules.name: Longitudinal Stationary Wave in Organ Pipe

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Longitudinal Stationary Waves in Organ Pipe: When two identical longitudinal progressive waves superpose while moving in opposite direction, then longitudinal stationary waves are formed

(1) Closed Organ Pipe (C.O.P.): - The tube which is closed at one end and open at the another end is called closed organ pipe.

• In closed organ pipe fundamental frequency is equal to $\dfrac{v_0}{4L}$.
    • Number of harmonics = (2 × overtone) + 1
    • Number of antinodes = m + 1, Number of nodes = m + 1
    • When closed organ pipe vibrate in mth overtone, then frequency $f = \left( (2 \times \text{m} + 1) \dfrac{v}{4L} \right)$
    • Frequency of harmonics is given by f1: f­2: f3 …. = 1: 3: 5....

(2) Open Organ Pipe (O.O.P.): - The tube which is open at both ends is called an open organ pipe.

• In open organ pipe fundamental frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{v}{2l}$

• When open organ pipe vibrates in mth overtone then
Number of harmonics = (overtone +1), Number nodes = m +1, Number of antinodes = m + 2

    • When open organ pipe vibrate in mth overtone, then frequency $f = \dfrac{(m+1)v}{2l}$

• Ratio of frequency of harmonics is given by f1 : f2 : f3 ..... = 1 : 2 : 3 ....

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Resonance Tube Experiment:

For first resonance: $\ell_1=\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$

For Second resonance $\ell_2=\dfrac{3 \lambda}{4}$

$\lambda=2\left(\ell_2-\ell_1\right)$

If the frequency of the fork be $t^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, then the speed of sound at $t^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is given by $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{f} \lambda=2 \mathrm{f}\left(\ell_2-\ell_1\right)$

The speed of sound waves at $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ in air is $\mathrm{v}_0=\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{t}}-0.61 \mathrm{t}\right) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec}$

Calculation of end Correction:

For first resonance: $\ell_1+\mathrm{e}=\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$

For Second Resonance: $\ell_2+\mathrm{e}=\dfrac{3 \lambda}{4}$

$\mathrm{e}=\dfrac{\ell_2-3 \ell_1}{2}[\mathrm{e}=0.6 \mathrm{r}, \text { where } \mathrm{r} \text { is radius of tube }]$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Sound Wave:

  • Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves.
  • They propagate through a medium by compressions and rarefactions.
  • Speed of sound depends on the medium's properties such as density and elasticity.
Sound waves can be classified in three groups according to their range of frequencies.

(1) Infrasonic Waves: Longitudinal wave having frequencies below 20 Hz are called infrasonic waves.

(2) Sonic Waves/Audible Waves: Longitudinal waves having frequencies lying between 20 Hz-20000 Hz are called audible waves.

(3) Ultrasonic Waves: Longitudinal waves having frequencies above 20000 Hz are called ultrasonic waves.

Equations of sound wave:

(A) Displacement wave form: $\mathrm{s}=\mathrm{s}_{\max } \cos (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t})$

(B) Pressure wave form: $\Delta \mathrm{p}=\Delta \mathrm{p}_{\max } \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{p}_{\max }=\mathrm{Bks}_{\max }$

Speed of Sound Wave:

$\mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\text { Elastic property }}{\text { inertial property }}} \quad \mathrm{v}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{E}}{\rho}}$

(a) In Solids: $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{Y}}{\rho}}$

(b) In Liquids: $\mathrm{v}_{\ell}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{\rho}}}$

Velocity of sound wave in air according to Newton

In isothermal process B (Bulk modulus) = P (Atmospheric pressure)

$\mathrm{v_g}=\sqrt{\dfrac{P}{\rho}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{1.01 \times 10^5}{1.3}}=279 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$

However, the experimental value of sound in air is 332 m/s which is much higher than that given by Newton’s formula.

Laplace’s Correction:

In order to remove the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental values of velocity of sound, Laplace modified Newton’s formula assuming that propagation of sound in air is adiabatic process, i.e. $\mathrm{B}=\gamma \mathrm{P}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\mathrm{B}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{7 \times 1.01 \times 10^5}{5 \times 1.3}}=332 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{sec}$

Which is in good agreement with the experimental value (332 m/s). This establishes that sound propagates adiabatically through gases.

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Wave:

A wave is a disturbance which transports energy and momentum both from one point to another without the transport of matter.

Wave Classification:

Some important terms connected with wave motion

(1) Wave length ($\lambda$): It is the distance between two successive crest or two successive troughs.

(2) Frequency($f/n)$: Number of cycle (number of complete wavelengths travelled through a point) completed by a particle in unit time.

(3) Time Period (T) : Time taken by wave to travel a distance equal to the wavelength

(4) Amplitude (A) : Maximum displacement of vibrating particle from its equilibrium position.

(5)Angular frequency (ω) : It is defined as,.$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi n$

(6) Phase: Phase is a quantity which contains all information related to any vibrating particle in a wave.

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx)$

$\text{Phase} \Rightarrow (\omega t - kx)$

(7) Angular wave number (k) : Angular wave number or propagation constant is denoted by$k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$. The S.I. unit of ‘k’ is radian/meter.

(8) Wave number($\bar{v}$): It is defined as number of waves in unit length of the wave pattern.

$\bar{v} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{k}{2\pi}$

(9) Wave velocity ($v$):The velocity with which the disturbance travel through the medium is called wave velocity.

$v = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$ or $v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} \Rightarrow V=n \lambda$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Wave Equation and Characteristics of Waves

Equation of Plane Progressive Wave:

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx + \phi)$

If $\phi=0$

$y = A \sin(\omega t - kx )$

Note:  If the wave is along –x direction, then there will be plus sign instead of minus sign inside the brackets in the above equation

$y = A \sin(\omega t + kx )$

Particle Velocity ($v_p$) in Plane Progressive Wave

$v_p = A \omega \cos(\omega t - kx)$

Slope of S.H.W. (Simple Harmonic Wave)

$v_p = -v \left( \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)$

$\left|v_p\right|_{\max }=A \omega$

$v_p=$ particle velocity

$v =$ wave velocity

Particle velocity = - (Wave velocity) × (Slope of the tangent at that point on the wave at that instant)

Relation between phase difference, path difference & Time difference

$\dfrac{\Delta \phi}{2\pi} = \dfrac{\Delta x}{\lambda} = \dfrac{\Delta t}{T}$

Acceleration of particle in plane progressive wave

$a_p = -A \omega^2 \sin(\omega t - kx)$

$a_p = -\omega^2 y$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Energy Power and Intensity of Waves:

(1)Wave transport energy when they propagate through a medium. The total kinetic energy K associated with moving particles in one wavelength is

$K = \dfrac{1}{4} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2 \quad \mu \rightarrow \text { mass peronit length }$

(2) Each element of the string has potential energy associated with it due to its displacement from the equilibrium position and the restoring forces from neighbouring elements

$U= \dfrac{1}{4} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2$

$E = U + K = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu \lambda (\omega A)^2$

Intensity: It is defined to be the power per unit area carried by a wave. Power is the rate at which energy is transferred by the wave.

$I = \dfrac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area}} \quad \text { Power }=\frac{\text { Energy }}{\text { time }}$

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \mu v A^2 \omega^2 / \text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2} \rho v A^2 \omega^2$

Speed of Mechanical Wave on String

Velocity of Transverse Mechanical Waves: Velocity of a transverse wave propagating along a string having tension T and mass per unit length µ, is given by

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\pi r^2 \rho}}$

Velocity of Transverse Mechanical Waves: Velocity of a transverse wave propagating along a string having tension T and mass per unit length μ,

$v=\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\pi r^2 \rho}}$

Key Points

  • If medium remains same then  $\rho$ and  v is constant .
$ I \propto A^2 \omega^2 \Rightarrow I \propto A^2 n^2 \quad(\omega=2 \pi n)$

  • If medium and frequency both are constant then $ \mathrm{I} \propto \mathrm{~A}^2$
  • If medium is same and  v  is constant then, intensity (I) $\propto \omega^2 A^2 $
  • $\text { Power }=\dfrac{\text { Enegy }}{\text { Time }}$$$
  • Intensity due to point source $ I=\dfrac{P}{4 \pi \mathrm{r}^2}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Effect of various quantities on speed of sound wave:

1. Effect of temperature:

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{w}}}} $

$\quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{~T}} $  (Temperature(T) is in Kelvin)

2.Effect of Relative Humidity: With increase in humidity, density of air decreases

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{s}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma \mathrm{P}}{\rho}}$

3.Effect of Pressure: $v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M_W}}$

So, pressure has no effect on velocity of sound in a gas as long as temperature remain constant.

4.Effect of Wind: - If air is blowing then the speed of sound changes. If the actual speed of sound is v and the speed of air is w, then the speed of sound in the direction in which air is blowing will be (v + w), and in the opposite direction it will be (v – w).

5.Effect of Frequency: The speed of sound is not affected by frequency. Sound waves of different frequencies travel at the same speed in air, though their wavelengths vary. If the speed depended on frequency, we wouldn’t be able to enjoy orchestras.

Sound is characterised by the following three parameters:

• Loudness • Pitch • Quality/Timbre

• Loudness: The quality of sound on the basis of which, sound is said to be high or low.

It depends on, (a) Shape and size of the source (b) Intensity of sound

According to Weber - Fechner the loudness of a sound of intensity I is given by:

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{L} \propto \log _{10} \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~L}_2-\mathrm{L}_1=\Delta \mathrm{L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1} \end{aligned}$

Unit of loudness - decibel (dB)

For zero decibel (0 dB) Loudness, Intensity is called threshold of hearing$(\mathrm{I_0})$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{L}_2-\mathrm{L}_1=\Delta \mathrm{L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}_2}{\mathrm{I}_1} \\ & \mathrm{~L}-0=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}_0} \\ & \mathrm{~L}=10 \log _{10} \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}_0}\left(\text { Where } \mathrm{I}_0=10^{-12} \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{m}^2\right) \end{aligned}$

Pitch: It is the sensation received by the ear due to frequency and is the characteristic which distinguishes a shrill (or sharp) sound from a grave (or flat) sound.

Quality (or timbre): - It is the sensation received by the ear due to 'waveform’. Two sounds of same intensity and frequency as shown in figure will produce different sensation on the ear if their waveforms are different.

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Principle of Superposition:

$\vec{y}_{\text{net}} = \vec{y}_1 + \vec{y}_2 + \vec{y}_3$

$y_1 = A_1 \sin(\omega t - k x_1)$,$y_2 = A_2 \sin(\omega t - k x_2)$

Resultant Amplitude

$A_{\text{resultant}}=\sqrt{A_1^2+A_2^2+2A_1A_2\cos\phi}$

Resultant Intensity

$I \propto A^2$

$I = I_1 + I_2 + 2 \sqrt{I_1} \sqrt{I_2} \cos \Delta \phi$

Interference for Sound Waves :

When the waves emitting from the coherent sources propagating in same direction are superposed over one another, then redistribution of energy takes place in the space and this phenomenon is called as interference.

  • CONSTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE
  • Phase difference $\Delta \phi
=2n\pi$, where n= 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,.....
  • Path difference $\Delta x=
 0, \, \lambda, \, 2\lambda, \, 3\lambda, \ldots, \, n\lambda$
$A_{\text{max}} = A_1 + A_2$

$I_{\text{max}} = \left( \sqrt{I_1} + \sqrt{I_2} \right)^2$

  • DESTRUCTIVE INTERFERENCE
  • Phase difference $\Delta \phi
=(2n+1)\pi$, where n= 0,1,2,3,4,5,....
  • Path difference  $\Delta x
 = \frac{\lambda}{2}, \frac{3\lambda}{2}, \frac{5\lambda}{2}, \ldots, \frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{2}$
$A_{\text{min}} = A_1 - A_2$

$I_{\text{min}} = \left( \sqrt{I_1} - \sqrt{I_2} \right)^2$

$\dfrac{I_1}{I_2}=\left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\dfrac{A_{\max }}{A_{\min }}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2$

$\text { Average intensity of interference pattern }=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{2}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2$

Degree of interference pattern (f) = f represents contrast effect (clarity of interference pattern)

$\mathrm{f}=\dfrac{\mathrm{I}_{\max }-\mathrm{I}_{\min }}{\mathrm{I}_{\max }+\mathrm{I}_{\min }} \times 100 \%$

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Beats :When two sound waves of nearly equal (but not exactly equal) frequencies travel in same direction, at a given point due to their superposition, intensity alternatively increases and decreases periodically. This periodic waxing and waning of sound at a given position is called beats.

$\text { Beat frequency } \Delta f=\left|f_2-f_1\right|$

$\text { Beat Time period } T_{\text {beat }}=\dfrac{1}{\left|f_2-f_1\right|}$

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{res}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}_1+\mathrm{f}_2}{2}$

$\text { Time for } I_{\max } \text { to } I_{\min }, t=\dfrac{T_{\text {beat }}}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2\left|f_2-f_1\right|}$

blocks.title: CORE CONCEPTS
blocks.text:
Stationary Waves: When two identical waves (transverse or longitudinal) propagating in opposite direction superimpose in bounded medium then the resultant wave is called stationary wave or standing wave.

It is of two types

(1) Transverse stationary waves

(2) Longitudinal stationary waves

According to the nature of Reflected surface, Reflection are of two types,

(1) Reflection from rigid end

$y_i = a \sin(\omega t - k x)$

$y_r =- a \sin(\omega t + k x)$

The stationary wave formed due to the superposition of the incident and reflected waves is:

$y=y_i+y_r=a \sin (\omega t-k x)-a \sin (\omega t+k x)$

Note: In such type of reflection incident and reflected waves have phase difference of $\pi$ and direction of propagation are opposite

(2) Reflection from free end

$y_i = a \sin(\omega t - k x)$

$y_r = a \sin(\omega t + k x)$

Rigid End Reflection:

$y=2 a \cos (\omega t) \sin (k x)$

Free End Reflection:

$y=2 a \sin (\omega t) \cos (k x)$

Note: In such type of reflection incident and reflected waves are in phase and direction of propagation are opposite.

Important Points:

Nodes are points of zero displacement, and antinodes are points of maximum displacement in a standing wave.

Distance between two successive nodes or successive antinodes is λ/2.

Distance between successive node to antinode or antinode to node is λ/4.

Overtone frequency: Frequency higher than fundamental frequency.

Harmonic frequency: Integer multiple of fundamental frequency

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Longitudinal Stationary Waves in Organ Pipe: When two identical longitudinal progressive waves superpose while moving in opposite direction, then longitudinal stationary waves are formed

(1) Closed Organ Pipe (C.O.P.): - The tube which is closed at one end and open at the another end is called closed organ pipe.

• In closed organ pipe fundamental frequency is equal to $\dfrac{v_0}{4L}$.
    • Number of harmonics = (2 × overtone) + 1
    • Number of antinodes = m + 1, Number of nodes = m + 1
    • When closed organ pipe vibrate in mth overtone, then frequency $f = \left( (2 \times \text{m} + 1) \dfrac{v}{4L} \right)$
    • Frequency of harmonics is given by f1: f­2: f3 …. = 1: 3: 5....

(2) Open Organ Pipe (O.O.P.): - The tube which is open at both ends is called an open organ pipe.

• In open organ pipe fundamental frequency $f_0 = \dfrac{v}{2l}$

• When open organ pipe vibrates in mth overtone then
Number of harmonics = (overtone +1), Number nodes = m +1, Number of antinodes = m + 2

    • When open organ pipe vibrate in mth overtone, then frequency $f = \dfrac{(m+1)v}{2l}$

• Ratio of frequency of harmonics is given by f1 : f2 : f3 ..... = 1 : 2 : 3 ....
